verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains falāḥ as success in attaining one’s aim, so called because it splits the barriers to the objective. It includes worldly benefits such as health, wealth, and honor, and otherworldly success: life without death, wealth without need, honor without humiliation, and knowledge without ignorance.

Īmān is to acknowledge and confirm God’s Oneness, His messengers and teachings, and the Last Day, while generally obeying their implications. The Qur’an therefore joins belief to righteous deeds. Mere knowledge or verbal acknowledgement is not īmān: īmān also requires conviction, and conviction entails practical compliance. One may know an evil while continuing it, just as Pharaoh’s people denied the signs despite inward certainty (27:14). Personal impediments or attractions may lead a believer to disobey some implications of faith, but īmān cannot be wholly without obedience.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan defines khushūʿ as a state in which a person, overpowered by a mighty being, is cut off from everything else and directs attention solely to that being. It is apparently a state of the heart, though it may extend to the limbs. The Prophet’s reported remark about a man playing with his beard in prayer—“Had his heart been humble (khashaʿa), his limbs would have also been humble”—illustrates this extension. Awe with stillness of the limbs, lowered gaze, bowed head, undistracted concentration, glorification of God, and manifest subservience are all included within this meaning.

The qualities in these verses are necessary effects of living, active īmān and thus bring the salvation for which īmān is meant. In prayer, one who is wholly needy turns toward God, the Source of might and greatness. Awareness of God’s station produces abasement before Him, detaches the heart from irrelevant concerns, and, where belief is genuine, leaves the worshipper wholly absorbed in his Lord. The Prophet reportedly told Ḥārithah b. al-Nuʿmān, “Surely there is a sign for every truth, and there is a light for every right.”

Religion is a practical social tradition founded on a worldview about existence and humanity. A society that believes in a creating and returning Lord and an eternal human life will order its conduct toward everlasting otherworldly happiness; one that believes in gods but not return to them will seek their favor for worldly well-being; and one that believes in neither God nor eternal life will organize itself around material pleasure ending in death.

A religious worldview is not merely theoretical knowledge, since knowledge alone does not compel practice. It is practical knowledge: knowing and deciding that one must follow a theory’s practical implications, such as worshipping God and observing what secures happiness in this world and the hereafter. Accordingly, īmān is commitment to the practical implications of belief in God, His messengers and teachings, and the Last Day.

Practical knowledge varies with the strength of motives. An incentive to act may be overridden by a stronger one, as hunger’s incentive to eat is qualified by the realization that a particular food is harmful. Likewise, faith produces righteous deeds and traits such as awe, humility, and sincerity only when wrong motives and devilish deceptions do not overcome it. Faith is effective when it is not conditional or circumstantial: “And among men is he who serves Allah (standing) on the edge (22:11).” A wholly unconditional believer acts according to faith’s implications, including humility in worship and turning away from vanity.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains al-laghw as an act without benefit, though benefit may differ by perspective. Religiously, it denotes permissible acts that bring neither otherworldly benefit nor a worldly benefit that continues to the hereafter; eating and drinking merely for pleasure, rather than for strength to serve God, is an example. More precisely, it is every act other than the obligatory and recommended acts (wājibāt and mustaḥabbāt).

The verse uses iʿrāḍ, turning away, rather than tark, absolute avoidance. Since people are liable to slips and God pardons lesser evil deeds when grave sins are shunned—“If you shun the great sins which you are forbidden, We will do away with your [lesser] evil deeds (4:31)”—believers are not described as never falling into vanity. Rather, their prevailing direction is away from it. Iʿrāḍ is an active refusal of what draws one because one does not regard it as significant.

Faith connects its possessor to God, the source of magnificence and nobility, and therefore raises the soul above base pursuits. The believer seeks the everlasting happy life and values what God deems great, not what ignorant and ignoble people prize. Thus, “And when the ignorant address them, they say: Peace (25:63),” and “And when they pass by what is vain, they pass by nobly (25:72).” Keeping aloof from vanity consequently describes the loftiness of their resolve and the nobility of their souls.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan holds that zakāh here denotes financial charity rather than purification from moral vices. Since the chapter is Meccan and zakāh later became, in Medina, a fixed term for the amount due, it is more likely used here as a verbal noun: purifying one’s wealth by spending part of it in God’s way, not the money paid itself.

This reading accords with calling believers “doers” (fāʿilūn) of zakāh: they actively help the poor financially. If zakāh meant the money itself, one would have to supply an omitted word, reading “doers of paying the zakāh”; some instead interpret it as purification of the soul to avoid this difficulty. The expression “doers” conveys particular attention and determination beyond merely calling them payers or fulfillers.

Belief in God calls for financial charity because complete happiness requires a felicitous society in which people receive their rights and social classes are brought closer in living standard and quality of life. Charity to the poor and less fortunate is among the most effective means of establishing this equity.
verses.5: Al-Mizan explains furūj as the private parts of men and women. Guarding them means abstaining from sexual intercourse, including adultery, sodomy, intercourse with animals, and similar acts.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that the verse excepts lawful wives (azwāj) and bondswomen from the command to guard one’s private parts; believers are not blameable for intercourse with either. A translator’s note adds that, although the wording primarily describes believing men, the passage concerns all believers, so believing women likewise do not sleep with an unlawful man.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains that the fāʾ makes this verse the consequence of the preceding exception: faith requires guarding one’s private parts absolutely except with wives and bondswomen. Whoever seeks intercourse beyond these lawful women is a transgressor who violates the limit God has set.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan takes amānah here to mean things entrusted to a person, such as property; its plural apparently refers to the various trusts exchanged among people. The broader interpretation that includes God’s trust—His rules and covenants, and the body and faculties to be used in His pleasure—is unlikely from the primary wording, though true after analysis and generalization.

In the shariah, ʿahd is a commitment made through a prescribed formula, alongside a nadhr or yamīn, but it may also encompass every duty imposed on a believer. The singular may therefore imply God’s single covenant of īmān, which includes all religious obligations. Riʿāyah means preserving and maintaining, whatever its original lexical application.

Thus believers protect trusts from breach and covenants from violation. This follows from īmān, which entails composure, confidence, and security: property left with a believer and an agreement made with one remain safe from loss through betrayal or breach.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains guarding the prayers as maintaining their number and order, being constantly mindful of them, and not missing any obligatory prayer; this is a necessary consequence of īmān. “Prayers” is plural here, whereas “prayer” was singular in (23:2) because khushūʿ applies equally to every prayer, making the singular a generic term that includes them all.
verses.10: Al-Mizan identifies Paradise (al-firdaws) as the highest of the heavenly gardens.
verses.11: Al-Mizan explains inheritance of Paradise as follows: all initially have the possibility of earning and entering it, but those who fail forfeit their prospective share, which the believers inherit. According to narrations, every person initially has a place in heaven and hell; when one enters hell after death, the people of heaven inherit that person’s place in heaven.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, that sulālah is something extracted from another thing. “Man” (al-insān) denotes the whole human species: Adam, initially fashioned from clay, and his progeny, whose creation continues through nuṭfah. Thus the verse and the following one correspond to: And He began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his progeny of an extract, of water held in light estimation (32:7-8).

The use in the next verse of jaʿl—Then We made him a drop (23:13)—rather than khalq confirms that both Adam and his descendants are intended. Were the passage concerned only with Adam’s progeny, it should have said that He fashioned him a drop, as khalq is used for the later transformations of the drop and clot. The verse therefore cannot be restricted either to Adam’s children, as though their clay-origin merely meant that their seed ultimately derives from earthly dust, or to Adam alone.

It is said that khalq originally means measuring (taqdīr), as one measures fabric for a garment. The verse consequently means that God first measured and fashioned humankind from an extract of earthly matter mixed with water, namely clay.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that nuṭfah means a small quantity of water, though it can also refer to water generally. Qarār, literally “placement,” is used emphatically in place of “resting-place” and denotes the womb. Makīn means firm or established: it may describe the womb’s protection of the drop from loss and damage, or the drop’s secure placement within it.

Thus, after first fashioning man from clay, God made him a drop in the firm resting-place of the womb, transforming the course of his creation from the former stage to this one.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan calls the clothing of the bones with flesh an elegant metaphorical expression. According to al-Rāghib, inshāʾ means to make and foster something, while nashʾ and nashʾah mean to originate and grow it. The shift from khalq, “fashioning,” to “then We caused it to grow into another creation” marks the appearance of something fundamentally new, unlike the preceding material transformations. Although a clot differs from a drop in such qualities as colour and taste, both retain the same kind of properties. At the final stage, however, God brings forth from non-existence a soul possessing life, knowledge, and power—the substantial reality called “I”—for which there is no equivalent in the stages of drop, clot, lump of flesh, bones, and flesh.

The pronoun in anshaʾnāhu refers to the human being whose bones have been clothed with flesh. This material body, previously devoid of life, knowledge, and power, is transformed into a being different in essence, attributes, and properties. It is the same being in one respect and not the same in another; the new creature is attached and united to the preceding matter, using the body as a writer uses a pen. This is supported by: And they say: What! When we have become lost in the earth, shall we then certainly be in a new creation? Nay! They are disbelievers in the meeting of their Lord. Say: The angel of death who is given charge of you shall fully capture you (32:10-11). At death, the person’s reality is fully captured, whereas the body disintegrates in the earth; they are not identical.

Some exegetes hold that thumma marks stages wholly distinct from what precedes them—making the drop, fashioning the clot, and causing another creation to grow—whereas fāʾ marks uninterrupted stages: the clot becoming flesh, flesh becoming bones, and bones being clothed with flesh.

Al-Rāghib explains barakah as the persistence and durability of divine good, and its usage also conveys an abundance beyond sensory observation, enumeration, and limit. God’s tabāraka therefore denotes the abundant good He exclusively bestows on creatures. Since khalq means measuring, God is “the best of the creators” because His proportioning of each being’s parts and of beings in relation to one another bestows existence and is the source of abundant good. The phrase also shows that khalq is not exclusive to God, for measuring and comparing are ascribed to others in: And when you [O Jesus] fashioned out of clay a thing like the form of a bird (5:110), and: And you create a lie (29:17).
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that death is a further stage completing God’s measured and determined plan for humankind. Every person must inevitably pass through it; death is certain.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that resurrection is the final stage of God’s plan for humankind. Once raised on the Day of Resurrection, they will remain and abide forever.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan identifies the seven ṭarāʾiq above humanity as the seven heavens. They are called ways because God’s command descends through them to earth, human deeds ascend through them to God, and angels descend and ascend by them. Thus, “never are We heedless of creation” means that people are neither cut off from God nor beyond His supervision: these seven ways connect them to Him through the descent and ascent of messenger angels, the descent of His command, and the ascent of their actions.

Some exegetes interpret ṭarāʾiq as superimposed layers, while others take tarīqah to mean something spread out and flattened. Al-Mizan objects that neither interpretation clearly connects the verse’s opening with its assertion that God is not heedless of creation.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that al-samāʾ here means what is above and overshadows people; the water sent down from it is rain. Its descent “according to a measure” follows God’s perfect, fixed plan, neither exceeding nor falling short by a single drop.

God then stores this water in the earth as groundwater in mountains and plains, from which springs, rivers, and wells arise. He is fully able to remove the stored water so that people would not know where it has gone or how to reach it.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains that, when used of gardens, inshāʾ means making and growing them: by this water God grows for people gardens of palm trees and grapes, containing abundant fruit from which they eat.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that the conjunction joins this tree to the preceding gardens: God causes it to grow by the water. It is the olive tree, which grows abundantly in Mount Sinai. Its fruit produces olive oil and ṣibgh, a condiment or seasoning added to food. The olive is singled out because of its peculiarity.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that cattle are a lesson in God’s direction of creation and His kindness, compassion, and mercy toward it. God gives people milk from their bellies, as well as other benefits such as wool, hair, fur, and skin, and provides them with their meat for food.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains that “them” refers to cattle, and being carried on them means riding camels, the means of travel on land. This contrasts with travel by sea on ships. Fulk is the plural of falakah, meaning “ship” (safīnah).
verses.23:
Al-Mizan identifies Noah as the first of the Resolute Messengers (ūlū al-ʿazm), sent with a book and law to all people of his age, to establish monotheism openly and abolish polytheism. Thus, “his people” means his entire nation.

Noah’s call to “serve Allah” required abandoning the angels, jinn, and human saints whom idolaters treated as gods. The commentary rejects the view that the verse merely omits an explicit qualification to worship God “alone.” The idolaters did not worship God alongside others: believing Him too exalted to be directly approached, they worshipped supposed intermediaries whom they thought governed their affairs and could bring them near to Him. Yet, had they thought God could properly be worshipped, they would have acknowledged that He alone must be worshipped, since they accepted Him as Lord of lords and the originator of all.

Accordingly, “you have no god other than Him” means that no other lord governs their affairs and therefore none deserves worship in hope or fear. The fāʾ in “will you not then guard [against evil]?” draws the conclusion: since there are no such lords, they should fear God’s punishment for refusing His worship and showing ingratitude.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains al-malaʾ as the chiefs and elite, and takes “of those who disbelieved” descriptively: none of Noah’s chiefs believed. Addressing the general public, they advanced contrived sophistries to turn people against Noah, silence his call, and incite trouble against him.

First, they argued that Noah was only a mortal like themselves. If revelation and connection to the unseen were a human perfection, they claimed, others like him should possess it; since they did not, he must be lying. They then alleged that his real aim was superiority and leadership through demanding obedience. Second, they argued that, if God wished to communicate from the unseen, He would have sent angels—the beings closest to Him and thought to intercede between humanity and Him. Their descent and repudiation of worship directed to them would, they claimed, have been a clear proof. The plural “angels” may allude to the many angels they had made gods. Third, they appealed to precedent: because their supposedly wiser forefathers had heard nothing like this, Noah’s call was an innovation and fabricated lie.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan treats this as the chiefs’ fourth argument against Noah. Jinnah may mean junūn, madness, or, if al-jinn is plural, that a jinn had possessed him and spoken through him. They regarded his teaching as something no sound mind could accept, and urged people to wait until he recovered or died.

These allegations, whether all voiced by the chiefs collectively or by different groups among them, were unsound dialectically but effective in alienating the people from Noah and keeping them in error.
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains this as Noah’s plea for help against his people’s denial. The bāʾ in bimā kadhdhabūni may mean, “Replace their denial with Your help,” or, more likely in light of their demand for the threatened punishment and Noah’s later prayer against the disbelievers, “Help me through the very warning they deny.” Its lack of a conjunction answers the implied question of how Noah responded to their accusations.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan reads God’s revelation as the answer to Noah’s plea. To build the ark “before Our eyes” is to build under God’s watch and protection, while building according to revelation means that its construction was taught to Noah step by step from the unseen.

“[W]hen Our command is given” is said to mean God’s decree settling the dispute by drowning Noah’s people. The oven’s gushing water signalled that punishment was imminent and was miraculous, since an oven is a place of fire. Noah was to bring into the ark one male and one female from every kind of animal. Although some objected that joining “your family” to “a pair” would make “of every kind” apply to the family, the commentary holds that min kullin qualifies zawjayn in meaning, so the conjunction creates no such difficulty.

Ahl denotes those specially connected to Noah, apparently including his household and believers. The exception of those against whom the word had gone forth was understood by Noah to concern his unbelieving wife, but in fact included his son, who chose a mountain over the ark and drowned; the word is the final decree of drowning. God’s command not even to speak to Him concerning the unjust is an emphatic prohibition of intercession, because His wrath and their drowning were irrevocably decreed.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan says that God teaches Noah, once settled in the ark, to praise Him for deliverance from the unjust, confirming that they will inevitably drown. Noah is also taught to ask for rescue from the flood and settlement in a blessed land of abundant, enduring good; God is the best of harborers, who settles people in the best manner.

The command that Noah praise and describe God indicates that he was among the chosen, purified servants (al-mukhlaṣīn), whom God excepts from the inadequate descriptions of others: Glory be to Allah [for freedom] from what they describe; but not so the servants of Allah, the purified ones (37:159-160). The narrative mentions the decree of drowning without recounting its occurrence, suggesting an obliteration so complete that no account remained. This silence itself conveys God’s immense power and wrath and the offenders’ insignificance more forcefully than an explicit report of their end.
verses.29:

Noah is also taught to ask for rescue from the flood and settlement in a blessed land of abundant, enduring good; God is the best of harborers, who settles people in the best manner.

This silence itself conveys God’s immense power and wrath and the offenders’ insignificance more forcefully than an explicit report of their end.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that the call of Noah and its ensuing events are signs and an instance of God’s ibtilāʾ: His testing and trial of humankind.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains qarn as a people living in one era. God’s sending of a messenger is elaborated through its result: the messenger calls his people to worship Allah alone, for they have no god besides Him, and to guard against evil.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains qarn as a people living in one era. God’s sending of a messenger is elaborated through its result: the messenger calls his people to worship Allah alone, for they have no god besides Him, and to guard against evil.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan describes these chiefs as worldly elites who sought to incite the public against their messenger. They disbelieved in God by serving other gods, denied the meeting of the hereafter, and, having thus cut themselves off from both origin and end, became immersed in material life. Their abundance and luxury attached them to wealth, display, and pleasure, so they opposed monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection in order to preserve their worldly ease and unrestricted pursuit of desire.

Their contemptuous appeal to the messenger’s eating and drinking was intended to deny his prophethood: a person sharing ordinary human and animal needs, they claimed, could have no distinction over others. This exposes their outlook that no perfection lies beyond animal nature and that happiness consists solely in freer and fuller carnal enjoyment. Thus they treated the messenger as a liar and the public as beings to be swayed by this materialistic standard.
verses.34: Al-Mizan takes this as equivalent to the earlier allegation that the messenger seeks superiority. Since he is, in their view, only a mortal with no advantage over them, obeying him would mean loss: it would surrender the freedom to pursue worldly pleasures, which they regard as the sole happiness, and amount to consenting to enslavement by an equal.
verses.35: Al-Mizan explains “brought forth” (mukhrajūn) as resurrection (mabʿūthūn) from the graves for reckoning and retribution.
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains hayhāta hayhāta as an exclamation of improbability; its repetition intensifies their denial that resurrection can occur.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains “we die and we live” primarily as the continuing worldly succession in which some people die and others come to life in their place. It may also refer to tanāsukh, the transmigration of a soul after death into another human or non-human body, a polytheist belief sometimes called birth after birth; however, this reading does not fit the context well. Their final claim denies resurrection into another abode after this world.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan says that after denying monotheism and the hereafter, the chiefs deny prophethood itself: both the messenger’s claim to be sent and the content of his message. “We” may include both chiefs and public, so that the chiefs do not appear merely to command the masses; or it may refer to the chiefs alone, declaring their position in order to lead the people after them.

Their charges arise from their disbelief in monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection, together with their indulgence in worldly luxury. The differing word order from Noah’s story is stylistic: placing “from among his people” before the successive descriptions preserves their sequence, while placing it after all of them would create too long a separation.
verses.39: Al-Mizan presents this as the messenger’s plea to his Lord for help against his people’s calling him a liar.
verses.40: Al-Mizan takes this reply as acceptance of the messenger’s plea. Their coming regret alludes to the exterminating punishment awaiting the people. ʿAmmā qalīl combines “after” with an intensifier of the short interval, while the emphatic form la-yuṣbiḥunna conveys a sworn certainty: after only a little while, punishment will overtake them and they will regret.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the Cry seized them with justice, either as a seizure accompanied by justice or as one caused by a just decree. Ghuthāʾ means the light debris borne by a flood, such as dry plants, leaves, and brushwood. Thus the heavenly Cry fulfilled the promise of punishment, reducing the unjust to floating refuse; “so away with” them means that they are cursed and far from God’s mercy, or is a prayer to that effect.

The people and their prophet are unnamed. Since they came after Noah’s people and were destroyed by a cry, the commentary considers it likely that they were Thamūd and their prophet Ṣāliḥ.
verses.42: Al-Mizan states that successive generations were raised after them, but no people can either hasten or postpone its appointed doom.
verses.43: Al-Mizan states that successive generations were raised after them, but no people can either hasten or postpone its appointed doom.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains tatrā as coming successively, one after another, with intervals between the members of the sequence. Thumma here continues the account rather than marking a temporal gap. The verse concisely covers the messengers and nations after Noah and the people destroyed by the Cry, up to Moses: God raised successive nations and sent each one its messenger, but each nation denied him.

“[W]e made some of them follow others” means that one nation succeeded another through the predecessor’s extermination. Making them “stories” means reducing once-living peoples to mere historical reports, an especially eloquent portrayal of wrath that erases the deniers’ outward existence and trace. “So away with” them means that the unbelievers are far from God’s mercy.

The verse displays God’s sunnah of raising generations and sending messengers as a test and trial. The generations’ recurring practice was to deny them, and God’s responding sunnah was to requite and punish the deniers successively.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains God’s “signs” as Moses’ staff, white hand, and other miracles shown to Pharaoh and his people. The “clear authority” is evident proof and argument, not, as some exegetes incorrectly claim, the staff.
verses.46: Al-Mizan notes the view that Pharaoh’s chiefs alone are named because the masses followed their leaders, though Moses and Aaron were sent to all of Pharaoh’s people. Their ʿuluww was their habitual pursuit of supremacy, expressed in oppressing and enslaving others, as they did the Children of Israel; elevation on earth is thus a metaphor for coercing people into obedience.
verses.47: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh and his chiefs argued both that Moses and Aaron, as mortals like themselves, had no superiority over them, and that Pharaoh’s side was superior because the prophets’ people served them. They therefore claimed that Moses and Aaron ought to serve them rather than be believed and followed. Their rejection ended in their destruction.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh and his chiefs argued both that Moses and Aaron, as mortals like themselves, had no superiority over them, and that Pharaoh’s side was superior because the prophets’ people served them. They therefore claimed that Moses and Aaron ought to serve them rather than be believed and followed. Their rejection ended in their destruction.
verses.49: Al-Mizan explains that “they” refers to the Children of Israel, not Pharaoh and his chiefs, since the latter had drowned before the Torah was revealed.
verses.50: Al-Mizan explains that Jesus and Mary constitute one sign because his extraordinary birth was a single miracle involving them both. God settled them in a residence on a broad, level, elevated rabwah, a secure resting place supplied with running water (maʿīn). Their shared sign manifests God’s lordship.
verses.51: Al-Mizan takes this as a general address to all messengers. “Eat of the good things” means use and benefit from good provisions generally, not only by ingestion, and expresses God’s favor toward them. They are therefore commanded to do good as gratitude for His blessings. “Surely I know what you do” both grounds the command, warns against disobedience, and calls them to taqwā (self-restraint, Godwariness, piety).
verses.52: Al-Mizan states that the messengers’ religion is one, God alone is their Lord, and they must therefore be careful of their duty to Him.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains that, although God sent successive messengers to a single community under one Lord and commanded watchfulness toward Him, people instead divided their religious affair and rejoiced in their respective portions. According to Majmaʿ al-bayān, zubur is the plural of zabūr, “book,” yielding the sense that they split religion into books, each party holding one.

The commentary prefers Ibn ʿĀmir’s recitation, zubarān, the plural of zubrah, meaning a division or sect: they divided into sects and parties, each exulting in what it possessed.
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains ghamrah, literally abundant water covering its bed, as a metaphor for ignorance that envelops a person. The command to leave them in it until an indefinite ḥīn threatens punishment: in accordance with God’s practice toward those who reject His messengers, it will arrive suddenly and unexpectedly.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that numidduhum derives from imdād, aid or extension, whose basic sense is to supply what is lacking and preserve something from loss. The disbelievers mistake the successive provision of wealth and children during their worldly respite for swiftly bestowed goods that prove God’s pleasure, approval, and esteem for them.

The reality is the reverse: this provision is istidrāj, respite through which they are led gradually toward destruction while wandering blindly in transgression. Thus they do not perceive that their apparent prosperity is not evidence of divine favor.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that numidduhum derives from imdād, aid or extension, whose basic sense is to supply what is lacking and preserve something from loss. The disbelievers mistake the successive provision of wealth and children during their worldly respite for swiftly bestowed goods that prove God’s pleasure, approval, and esteem for them.

The reality is the reverse: this provision is istidrāj, respite through which they are led gradually toward destruction while wandering blindly in transgression. Thus they do not perceive that their apparent prosperity is not evidence of divine favor.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that the believers described in these verses, unlike disbelievers who take wealth and children for hastened good, hasten toward the true good: belief in God, His messengers, and the Final Day, together with righteous action.

Ishfāq combines care (ʿināyah) with fear (khawf); when followed by min, its fearful aspect is especially prominent, whereas fī emphasizes care. Calling God “their Lord” shows that they acknowledge Him as the Director of their affairs and regard their salvation and damnation as dependent on His pleasure and wrath. They therefore fear Him concerning what they dearly seek—salvation and felicity—and this concern leads them to believe in His communications and serve Him. Khashyah and ishfāq are consequently not redundant.
verses.58: Al-Mizan takes āyāt here to mean everything that signifies and points to God: His messengers, the scriptures and supporting signs, and the divine laws they bring. Fearful caution before God moves believers to seek His satisfaction, accept His call, and obey the commands conveyed through revelation and the messengers.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan connects the believers’ refusal to associate anything with their Lord to their belief in God’s communications. Those communications include both the shariah, which commands worship of God alone, and proofs of His Oneness in lordship and worship.

Moreover, lordship entails sending messengers to guide subjects to salvation. If God had a partner, that partner too should have sent messengers, yet no messenger has come from other gods. Imam ʿAlī is reported to have said: “If your Lord had a partner, then surely his messengers would have come to you.”
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains wajal as fear. “Those who give what they give” primarily denotes giving alms in God’s way, though it may include every righteous deed. They give, or perform righteous deeds, with hearts fearful because they will return to their Lord; remembrance of that inevitable return, joined to fear, motivates their action.

The verse thus includes belief in the Last Day and righteous practice, completing the believers’ qualities: belief in God without association, belief in His messengers, belief in the Last Day, and righteous deeds.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan apparently takes the lām in lahā to mean “toward,” marking the goal of the race: the believers hasten to good things, namely righteous deeds, and compete to be foremost in them. An alternative rendering takes sābiqūn as winners in the race and lahā as referring to the good things that they attain.

The passage clarifies that the good things denied to the disbelievers in 23:55-56 are righteous deeds founded on true belief, along with their good rewards; they are not wealth and children. Al-Rāzī reports two possibilities: the believers zealously rush to obedience before the opportunity passes, or benefits and honors are hastened to them, which is equivalent to their hastening toward those benefits. He favors the latter because it affirms for believers what was denied of disbelievers.

Al-Mizan holds that al-Rāzī still must explain why this verse attributes hastening to believers rather than to God, and rejects the suggestion that the change merely shows that they deserve the good by their deeds. The present verse naturally speaks of believers’ own haste; what needs explanation is the earlier attribution of hastening to God, since wealth and children came to the disbelievers by God’s bestowal rather than their acquisition. The earlier rhetorical question negates their false supposition, while this verse affirms its proper opposite for believers: wealth and children are not the good sought, disbelievers do not hasten toward good, and believers hasten toward righteous deeds and their rewards.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan treats the verse as encouragement to acquire the believers’ qualities and as removing two deterrents: these qualities are within people’s capacity, and God neither loses their righteous acts nor defaults on their reward.

God imposes no religious obligation beyond a soul’s ability. In belief, He supplies proofs and signs and gives people intellects whose capacities differ; He therefore requires from each person according to that capacity, not demanding of the general public what He demands of the elite, of al-abrār what He demands of al-muqarrabūn, or of the disadvantaged what He demands of the chosen. In practice, religion serves human good in individual and social worldly life and eternal felicity, and creatures are equipped to move toward the good that completes them. Its duties therefore contain no undue burden serving an undue end.

The wording also negates both an inherently undue duty, such as monasticism (rahbāniyyah) or sacrificing one’s child, and an otherwise ordinary duty made impossible by an individual’s circumstances, such as standing for prayer when one cannot stand. Because nafsan is indefinite in a negative construction, this applies universally to every soul in every circumstance. The verse consequently implies differing degrees of belief according to intellectual capacity, as well as the absence of undue obligations in themselves or in their particular application.

The book with God “speaks the truth” because the very deeds are recorded in it and its account admits neither addition, omission, nor distortion. Reckoning and reward rest on this record, so no reward can be forgotten, withheld, reduced, altered, or lost.

Al-Rāzī raises the objection that one who regards divine lying as impossible needs no book to trust God’s statement, while one who considers it possible cannot trust the book; he answers that God does what He wills and that the record may benefit the recording angels. Al-Mizan rejects this answer as resting on a view that denies real purposes in God’s acts and permits arbitrary, purposeless will. The objection would also undermine the other eschatological stages of gathering, witnesses, records, the bridge, scales, and reckoning. These stages portray the return to God by the analogy of a court, where judgment requires evidence and proof; nevertheless, deeds manifest to a person at that return only by God’s will and permission.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan explains ghamrah as an engulfing, intense heedlessness or ignorance. “This” most plausibly refers to the believers’ qualities and their haste toward good, though it may refer to the Qur’an, as the later mention of recited communications suggests.

The disbelievers instead perform deeds unlike those of believers: evil acts and vices that occupy them and prevent them from pursuing righteous deeds and good things.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains juʾār as the frightened cry of wild animals, used here metaphorically for a loud appeal for help. Although some exegetes take it as a moan of pain, the following verses favor the sense of crying for help.

The punishment particularly overtakes the affluent because the earlier provision of wealth and children concerned their well-off chiefs; the rest of the people follow them.
verses.65: Al-Mizan notes the shift from third-person description to direct second-person address. It intensifies the rebuke and cuts off the disbelievers’ hope of rescue through their cries, or through any other wish. A direct declaration from the One from whom help comes more decisively excludes aid than an indirect announcement through His agents that neither supplication nor intercession will help them.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains tankiṣūna as turning back, sāmir as speaking by night, and hujr or hajr as nonsensical speech. Sāmir may serve as singular or plural, though the plural recitation summaran is preferred; summāran is another intensified plural recitation.

The unconnected opening of the verse explains why they will receive no help: when God’s communications were recited to them, they arrogantly turned away and held nightly gatherings in which they babbled nonsense about the matter. The view that bihi refers to the House or the haram is unlikely.
verses.67:

verses.68:
Al-Mizan begins here the refutation of the disbelievers’ excuses for rejecting the Qur’an and the Prophet’s call. The rhetorical question asks why, amid their heedlessness and distractions, they did not ponder “the speech,” the Qur’an recited to them. Had they reflected on it, they would have recognized it as true speech from God and believed.

The following “or” is not conjunctive but transitional, meaning “rather”: has something come to them that did not come to their forefathers, so that it is a novelty to be rejected? Mere novelty does not itself prove falsehood. Yet divine religion is guidance for all people and times; if a purported religion had no equivalent among earlier humanity, it could not be part of God’s universal guidance, and that would decisively establish its falsity.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains recognizing a messenger as knowing his identity and lineage and being generally familiar with his inherited and acquired moral and psychological qualities. Such knowledge shows that he is truthful, believes in his call, and is supported by God.

The people knew the Prophet before his mission: an orphan who had lost both parents, unable to read or write, and not educated by a teacher. They had seen in him nothing blameworthy, repugnant to sound nature or reason, or suggestive of ambition for kingdom, wealth, or power. He then came reciting a book, calling to salvation and felicity, and bringing teachings and commands that astonish the intellect and a religion that amazes minds. They thus knew him through these distinctive miraculous qualities. Had they known him to lack them or possess their opposite, refusing his religion would have been a valid excuse, since submitting to such a person would violate reason.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains that the charge of madness is not answered by a bare denial but by its implication: the Prophet brought the truth, whereas they lie in making madness an excuse for unbelief. Their real reason for turning away is their aversion to the truth.

The verse also implicitly refutes the charge. If he were mad, his speech would be confused, senseless, and disordered, like the speech of one who neither knows what he wants nor understands what he says. But his message is wholly true and calls only to truth. The qualification “most of them” leaves aside socially insignificant mustaḍʿafīn whose attraction or aversion to truth did not matter in the eyes of the majority.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers’ aversion to truth means that they want the message of truth to conform to their desires. Were they left to believe and act as they wished, they would worship idols, posit multiple lords, reject revelation and the hereafter, and commit whatever indecency, iniquity, and mischief they desired. But if truth could follow their wishes in legislation, it could equally follow them in the order and creation of the universe. Their changing, unbounded desires would then destroy the fixed laws and order of the heavens, earth, and all within them.

More fundamentally, human beings belong to the interconnected order of creation. Like every species, humanity has a perfection and a path suited to its faculties and means; its path to eternal felicity consists in right beliefs and actions. Religion (dīn) is this path, grounded both in the universal order of creation and in the human fiṭrah (primary nature, innate disposition). Thus the true human way is a consequence of al-ḥaqq, comprising the real system governing the universe and the human constitution within it. Creation and direction are inseparable, as are the order of existence and religious law. A baseless law shaped by desires would require a corresponding corruption of the causal and ordered connections of creation.

The “reminder” (dhikr) is the Qur’an. It may remind people of God or of true beliefs and righteous deeds; the latter better suits the argument. Although all divine religions call to truth, the Qur’an gives the true path in its final and most elaborated form. Its being called “their” reminder means that it is the religion specifically sent to this community; turning from the Qur’an is therefore turning from their own religion. Some exegetes take the ascription as one of honor and glory. Al-Mizan acknowledges that the Qur’an honored the Prophet, his household, the Arabs, and his nation, but rejects this as the reason for the ascription here, since the context instead indicates the religion specifically addressed to them.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains kharj and kharāj as a payment collected as a due. The verse answers and rebukes a fourth excuse: the claim, in effect, that the Prophet asks them for a compulsory financial payment. God’s recompense is better, however; He provides for the Prophet, who has no need of their payment and is financially solvent.

This completes the stated refutations of their excuses: failure to ponder the Qur’an, treating the proposed religion as unprecedented, alleging madness in the Prophet, and objecting to his manner of calling on the ground that he seeks recompense.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains nakab and nukūb as deviation from a path and turning aside. The straight path is clear, internally non-contradictory, and unobstructed from attaining its destination. This is the character of truth: it is a unified reality whose parts do not contradict or frustrate one another and which reaches its end. Since the Prophet guides to truth, he guides to a straight path; since the disbelievers recoil from truth, they deviate from that path.

Their denial of the hereafter is singled out because true religion rests on an everlasting human life beyond death, with felicity earned by true belief and righteous deeds and wretchedness to be avoided. Alternatively, religion consists of binding beliefs and practices that require examination and requital, for which the Day of Resurrection exists. Those who deny it regard religion as vain, restrict happiness to material and carnal enjoyment, and follow desire whether or not it agrees with truth.

The commentary concludes that they will never believe the Prophet because he calls them to the straight path while they care only to depart from it.

verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains lajāj as stubborn persistence in a prohibited course, ʿamah as confused hesitation, and istakānah as seeking a state of khuḍūʿ, humility. If God mercifully removed the disbelievers’ distress, they would not gratefully return to truth but would persist in rebellion and wander blindly. Nor did chastisement benefit them: they failed to humble themselves before their Lord or plead for help. Thus neither relief nor calamity brings them to the straight path.

The failure to submit under chastisement does not conflict with the human tendency to turn to God when all apparent means are cut off, because the chastisement here is a lighter punishment that does not sever every means of hope. The verses indicate that a punishment had already befallen them and had not yet been removed; perhaps it was the drought that struck Mecca, as narrations report.

Nor did chastisement benefit them: they failed to humble themselves before their Lord or plead for help. Thus neither relief nor calamity brings them to the straight path.

The verses indicate that a punishment had already befallen them and had not yet been removed; perhaps it was the drought that struck Mecca, as narrations report.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that neither mercy nor the earlier chastisement benefits them until a door of severe chastisement is opened upon them. They will then be suddenly overcome by despair and lose all hope of good. In context, this severe chastisement is death and the punishments of the hereafter that follow it.

The sequence beginning at (23:68) therefore ends, like the preceding sequence beginning at (23:55), with punishment in the hereafter, a subject that continues in the following verses.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains that ears and eyes, distinctive faculties of animal life, raise creatures above simpler beings: they discern benefit and harm and move voluntarily toward what they desire and from what they dislike. Hearing and sight may be singled out because they suffice for the proof.

The “hearts” are the human faculty of intellection and understanding. Intellect vastly extends sensory powers, enabling people to know present and absent things, past and present realities, and the properties of objects directly or through instruments; it also rises above particulars to universal laws, theoretical knowledge, and absolute truths. These originated faculties disclose God’s amazing plan and cannot be adequately thanked for. “Little” (qalīlan) rebukes the audience: their gratitude is little, with “gratitude” understood as the omitted object described by qalīlan.
verses.79: Al-Mizan cites al-Rāghib that dharʾ is God’s making creatures manifest as individual beings, while ḥashr is bringing a group forth and moving it collectively. After making people sensitive and intelligent, God made them appear as earthly creatures; He will then gather and return them to meet Him.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as the next stage after humanity’s earthly appearance and eventual gathering to God. Intelligent life requires life, while resurrection requires death; hence God gives life and causes death. Life followed by death also requires time, expressed by the succession of night and day through which a lifespan reaches its appointed end. The alternation may additionally mean their differing lengths, producing seasons by which animals are fed and their lives maintained: And He made therein its foods, in four periods: alike for the seekers (41:10).

Together, the three verses outline human existence: the origination of senses and intellect requires corporeal life on earth until an appointed term; this requires life and death, temporal duration, and provision. Since creation belongs to God, the direction of affairs (tadbīr)—the causal order governing things according to their created relations—also belongs inseparably to Him. He is therefore their Lord, to whom they return. The closing question rebukes the disbelievers and calls them to awaken and believe.
verses.81: Al-Mizan explains “Nay” as moving from the implied answer that they do not understand to their actual speech. Their comparison with the ancients exposes blind adherence to forefathers as what keeps them from truth and leads them to deny the hereafter, thereby rendering religion useless. It also indicates that attachment to earthly life and materialism has been a continuing practice from the beginning and will remain so.
verses.82: Al-Mizan explains that this specifies the preceding “they say”: their question whether dust and bones can be raised conveys doubt and a sense that resurrection is unlikely.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” denotes resurrection, and “before” qualifies the claim that they had already been promised it. Asāṭīr means fables or superstitious stories. Although resurrection is referred to in the singular, it comprises such events as reviving, gathering, mustering, reckoning, heaven, hell, reward, and punishment; hence it is called “fables” in the plural.

They argue that prophets have long promised and threatened the Hour, and that, had it been true, it would already have occurred. Their appeal to this old promise is intended to establish their conclusion that it is mere fable. Thus their former doubtful question becomes firm, though weakly grounded, denial.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan says this begins arguments for resurrection based on God’s absolute ownership, lordship, and sovereignty. The idolaters addressed denied resurrection but accepted God as Creator and ultimate Lord of the lords and gods they worshipped, so His existence is assumed.

The question concerns real ownership (al-milk al-ḥaqīqī), not conventional ownership (al-milk al-iʿtibārī). In real ownership, the owned thing depends in every respect on its owner and cannot stand independently; conventional ownership is a social arrangement that may be valid or invalid and may be transferred. Real existential ownership identifies the source of authority and control in creation.
verses.85: Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters must concede that the earth and all on it belong to God, since they acknowledge Him as their sole creative cause and effects cannot exist independently of their cause. “Will you not then mind?” rebukes them for not seeing that the Owner who takes their lives has the authority and control to revive them.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan explains the mighty Throne (al-ʿarsh) as the central position of universal authority, where affairs are managed, events orchestrated, and every being’s reign held. Its greatness is marked by “mighty” and by the repeated “Lord.”

The commentary rejects the view that rabb simply means mālik. A rabb is an owner who controls its possession and directs its affairs. The previous question could elicit the idolaters’ admission of God’s ownership because creation entails ownership, even though they attributed lordship over the earth to other gods. The same distinction raises the question why they are said to acknowledge God as Lord of the heavens when many polytheists assigned heavenly bodies or beings to other gods.

Al-Mizan answers that polytheists lacked one agreed, systematic doctrine. Some, including Sabeans, Hindus, and Buddhists, distributed cosmic regions and species among gods whom they worshipped for intercession, representing them with idols. But many dispersed peoples, apparently including pre-Islamic Arabs, had no such structured system: some attached other gods or idols to the earth, while regarding the heavens, their inhabitants, and the seas as subject to God. They held that angels under God’s lordship were lords over what lay below them. Thus, if the verse addresses Arab polytheists—as apparently it does—their acknowledgment of God’s lordship over the seven heavens is true.

Even if it addresses groups assigning other gods to the physical heavens, “heavens” means the transcendent celestial realm, where affairs are determined and decrees descend, including its angels and jinn. The mighty Throne confirms this reading, since it is the source of universal laws governing even their supposed gods; they acknowledged Allah alone above that station. The verse thus asks who is Lord of that realm and of the Throne, and whether they acknowledge that their gods and those subject to them belong to God and possess only what He has granted them.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains that they acknowledge the seven heavens and the mighty Throne as Allah’s. They are therefore reproached for disregarding His wrath by denying resurrection, treating it as ancient fable, and mocking the messengers who warn of it. Since the source of the divine command belongs to Him, He can command the resurrection and second creation of humanity. The wording “Allah’s” refers to ownership rather than lordship, because acknowledging His ownership alone completes the argument.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains malakūt as emphatic mulk, rule or dominion. Whereas a mālik owns property, a malik owns both the owner and the property, exercising authority over both. The malakūt of each thing is its existence given by God’s creative command (amr), “Be” (kun), as indicated by: His command, when He intends anything, is only to say to it: Be, so it is. Therefore glory be to Him in Whose hand is the kingdom (malakūt) of all things (36:82-83). Thus God alone creates every thing, His authority encompasses all things and is binding and irrevocable over them.

“Who gives refuge, but against Him there is no refuge” excludes the possibility that created causes can oppose or prevent His will. He gives whatever bestowal He wills and may limit one of His actions only through another of His actions; every cause acts subject to His control and has only the effect He grants it. He can protect beings from one another, but nothing can protect a being if He wills it harm. The question therefore asks the resurrection-deniers who alone creates all things with their traits and effects and grants protection without any protection being possible against Him.
verses.89: Al-Mizan takes siḥr here metaphorically: bewitchment is the appearance of something contrary to its true form. Though they admit that the kingdom is Allah’s, they are reproached because truth appears to them as falsehood. Absolute sovereignty means that God can bring about a second creation and restore the dead for reckoning and retribution by the single creative command, “Be!” (kun). The three preceding arguments establish both resurrection’s possibility and God’s Oneness in lordship, since real ownership necessarily entails authority and control, which define a rabb.
verses.90: Al-Mizan explains that “Nay” follows the implied negation established by the preceding arguments. Since the polytheists acknowledge premises that prove resurrection, the messengers’ promise is not false: God has brought them truth through His messengers, while they lie in their claims and in denying resurrection.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan explains that the denied sonship is “real filiation”: a child derived by separation from the Divine and sharing in divinity, as idolaters attributed to some angels, jinn, and human saints, and as Christians claimed in saying, The Messiah is the son of Allah (9:30). It is not merely “claimed filiation,” adopting or calling an existing being a son to honor it, as in We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones (5:18). Such a claim is also impermissible, but it is not the subject here because it does not require divinity. The verse moves from the particular denial of a son (walad) to the broader denial of any god (ilāh), since not every alleged god was called God’s son.

Multiple gods would have to be distinct and independently direct their respective domains. Each would separate with what it created, leaving no unified, connected, and consistent order among humanity, animals, plants, land, sea, earth, and heaven. Yet creation is governed by a unified system whose components are coordinated and compatible.

The verse also rejects a hierarchy of gods. Systems of direction may be parallel (ʿarḍī) or vertical and causal (ṭūlī), with general systems supporting particular subordinate ones. A subordinate system cut off from its superior would perish. But if a supposed lower god depended on a higher one for its authority, actions, effects, and direction, it would be merely a means employed in administration, not an independent god. Its dependence contradicts the independence required by the polytheists’ own premise.

The commentary rejects explanations that treat the contradiction as arising because the lesser gods would be contingent beings (mumkin) rather than necessary beings (wājib). The idolaters themselves regarded only Allah as self-existent, while viewing their gods as contingent directors over lower planes. It likewise rejects readings based on premises absent from the verse, and the claim that the proof is only a public, persuasive argument rather than a decisive rational one.

Although the idolaters viewed their gods as directors rather than creators of the universe, direction includes forms of creating particulars within a general system. Thus each god was effectively a creator in its lower realm, while ījād, the giving of existence itself, belongs exclusively to God. The verse closes by declaring Allah transcendent above their descriptions.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that “the Knower of the unseen and the seen” qualifies Allah in the preceding verse and shows that He knows His own transcendence from their polytheistic descriptions. It is therefore an argument against partners: God bears witness that He knows no partner for Himself, like “Allah bears witness that there is no god but He” (3:18). “So may He be exalted” concludes the preceding proofs against association.

The commentary rejects the view that the verse instead proves that multiple gods would overpower one another or be deficient through ignorance. Such arguments only show that several gods cannot all be self-existent, whereas the idolaters affirmed self-existence only for God; moreover, some of their premises are disputable.
verses.93: Al-Mizan explains that, after recounting the polytheists’ associationism, denial of resurrection, and mockery of messengers, God threatens them with punishment and orders the Prophet to seek protection should he witness it. The repeated “My Lord” intensifies the plea. Immā is in-mā, with mā serving to reinforce the stressed nūn of turiyannī, so the wording means, in effect, “If You indeed show me.” Because he asks to be made to see what they are threatened with, the threat apparently includes worldly punishment.
verses.94: Al-Mizan explains that being placed “among” the unjust means being subjected to their punishment along with them.
verses.95: Al-Mizan reads this as comforting the Prophet: God assures him that He can show him the punishment threatened to the polytheists. It perhaps refers to their punishment at the Battle of Badr, which the Prophet and believers witnessed and by which their burning resentment was healed.
verses.96: Al-Mizan explains that evil must be repelled by the best available good: return offense with the best good one can do; if that is impossible, do some good; if even this is impossible, overlook the offense. “We know best what they describe” consoles the Prophet, who should not be grieved by the polytheists’ insolence toward God and His religion, for God knows it fully.
verses.97: Al-Mizan says the Prophet is commanded to seek his Lord’s refuge from the devils’ deceptions and their presence. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports that hamzah is a forceful push or repulsion, and a devil’s hamzah is its thrust toward sin through deceptive temptation. Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that hamazāt are the devils’ whispers that cross the heart. Their whispers and presence are implicitly identified as causes of the polytheists’ denial of religion and association of partners with God.
verses.98: Al-Mizan says the Prophet is commanded to seek his Lord’s refuge from the devils’ deceptions and their presence. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports that hamzah is a forceful push or repulsion, and a devil’s hamzah is its thrust toward sin through deceptive temptation. Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that hamazāt are the devils’ whispers that cross the heart. Their whispers and presence are implicitly identified as causes of the polytheists’ denial of religion and association of partners with God.
verses.99: Al-Mizan explains that “Until” marks the polytheists’ persistence in associating partners with God and attributing to Him what does not befit Him, while wealth and children delude them, until death overtakes one of them. “Send me back” (irjiʿūni) is apparently addressed in the plural to the angels who seize the soul, while “my Lord” is an aside expressing his appeal to God. The alternatives—that the plural addresses God respectfully or expresses repeated requests—are rejected because such plural usages are respectively uncommon and even more uncommon in God’s speech.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that laʿalla expresses the dying polytheist’s hope, prompted by the punishment now confronting him, that he may do good with the possessions he left behind by spending them charitably and in what pleases God. The broader interpretation—doing every kind of worship and obedience in the world left behind—is acceptable, but the first meaning is more immediate.

“By no means” rejects his return: his plea is only an ineffectual utterance. Barzakh is a barrier, and warāʾihim here means what lies ahead, confronting and encompassing them as the future seeks a person. It is the realm of the grave, the imaginal world (ʿālam al-mithāl), in which one lives after death until the Hour; narrations concerning it are abundant through both Shia and Sunni transmissions.

The alternative that barzakh merely blocks their return to this world is rejected. The qualification “until the day they are raised” indicates a barrier extending from this world to resurrection, not one located behind them, and would otherwise be irrelevant. Moreover, it would make the denial of return only temporary, whereas the unconditional refusal is conveyed by “By no means.” A translator’s note suggests that barzakh may both lie ahead until resurrection and prevent return to worldly life, while acknowledging that Al-Mizan’s reading is preferred.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan holds that this is the second blast of the Trumpet, which raises the dead, not the first blast that kills the living; the ensuing annulment of ties, questioning, and weighing all belong to resurrection. The negation of kinship means that worldly familial and social bonds have no efficacy there. Such bonds arise from worldly needs and enable mutual help, but the hereafter is the abode of the results and recompense of deeds, not of effective worldly means, including deeds themselves.

Not asking one another denotes the most evident function of relationships: inquiring in order to give or obtain help. This does not conflict with verses depicting people questioning one another, since this verse concerns reckoning and judgment, whereas those verses concern the inhabitants of Paradise or hell after they have reached their eternal abodes.
verses.102: Al-Mizan explains that those whose mawāzīn are heavy succeed, while those whose mawāzīn are light lose their souls and remain in hell. Mawāzīn may be the plural of mīzān, “scale,” or of mawzūn, “what is weighed,” namely the deeds weighed on that day.
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains that those whose mawāzīn are heavy succeed, while those whose mawāzīn are light lose their souls and remain in hell. Mawāzīn may be the plural of mīzān, “scale,” or of mawzūn, “what is weighed,” namely the deeds weighed on that day.
verses.104: Al-Mizan reports that Majmaʿ al-bayān distinguishes lafḥ from the gentler nafḥ: lafḥ is the fiercer striking of the face, like a simoom. The fire’s flames will strike their faces so that their lips contract and shrink, exposing their teeth; this is kulūḥ, the severe affliction described in the verse.
verses.105: Al-Mizan says they will be told: God’s communications were recited to them, but they rejected them.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that shiqwah, shaqāwah, and shaqāʾ are the opposites of saʿādah, the particular good or felicity proper to a thing. Their saying that “our adversity overcame us” means that wretchedness defeated and subdued them. By attributing it to themselves, they acknowledge responsibility: it arose through their evil choices, as their promise to do good if released presupposes their free capacity to choose good deeds.

This does not mean that their souls were essentially evil. Saying they were “overcome” shows that the human soul is originally simple and pure, capable of receiving either felicity or adversity; in their case adversity subsequently occupied it. Their statement therefore admits both that they have no excuse for rejecting the communications and that their wretchedness was acquired rather than essential.

Their admission that they were an erring people reinforces this confession, but is an attempt to escape punishment and return to acquire salvation. They treat acknowledgment as though it were repentance in the world, although the Day of Resurrection is a day of recompense, not action. Thus their confession expresses ingrained dispositions, like their continued lying and denial despite the truth’s becoming manifest to them.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains that their real request is to be returned to the world; being taken out of hell is only the means to that end. They seek to perform good deeds so that, after acknowledging their sin and repenting, they may be among those who repent and do good.
verses.108: Al-Mizan explains that ikhsaʾū is used metaphorically. Its literal use is to rebuff and shoo a dog with disdain; here it means that they are driven away, kept at a distance, and denied speech with God.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan identifies these servants as believers in God and His religion during worldly life. Belief is a return and repentance to God, and their request for forgiveness and mercy seeks the special mercy granted to believers: divine assistance to perform righteous deeds, attain felicity, and enter Paradise. Calling God “the best of the merciful” appeals for the granting of this request.

The believers and disbelievers make the same essential plea—repenting and seeking salvation—but differ in when they make it. Believers make it in this world; disbelievers defer it until the hereafter.
verses.110: Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers are addressed and the believers are the ones mocked. “My remembrance” is the believers’ worldly remembrance of God through their prayer, “O our Lord! We believe, so do Thou forgive us and have mercy on us,” corresponding to the disbelievers’ later remembrance in hell. The disbelievers were distracted from this remembrance by their absorption in mocking the believers. Although the wording makes the believers seem to have caused their forgetfulness, what truly caused it was the act of mockery; the expression shows that, for the disbelievers, their only relation to the believers was ridicule.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains that “this day” is the Day of Retribution. The believers are rewarded because they patiently maintained God’s remembrance despite the disbelievers’ mockery, and “they are the achievers” means that they alone, not their mockers, achieve success.

These verses thus finally deprive the disbelievers of hope that confession and a request to return can save them. Such repentance and action could benefit them only in the material world, the abode of action. The believers used them there and endured ridicule, while the disbelievers substituted mockery for them. Now, in the abode of recompense, believers receive the result of their deeds and the disbelievers are left empty-handed; it is too late for action to repair their wrongdoing.
verses.112: Al-Mizan explains that God’s question concerns how long people remained in the earth, that is, in their graves. Other verses about their claiming to have tarried only an hour establish this meaning, excluding interpretations that refer to their worldly lifetime or to the combined duration of worldly life and barzakh.
verses.113: Al-Mizan explains that their answer, “a day or part of a day,” expresses how short their stay in the earth appears when compared with the eternal life now before them. Similar verses describe it as an hour, or an afternoon or morning. “Ask those who keep account” means that they cannot calculate it and refer the question to those who have its record, likely the angels who count the days.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan explains that God confirms that they remained in their graves only a little while. The phrase “had you but known” has the force of a wish: if, while in the world, they had known that their grave-stay would be brief before resurrection, they would not have denied resurrection and incurred everlasting punishment. Divine expressions of wishing or hoping indicate ignorance or uncertainty in creatures or their situation, not in God.

The commentary rejects the claim that law introduces an omitted conditional main clause, since the proposed completion is contrived and incompatible with the context. It also rejects reading law as “even if” or “although,” for that reading would require connection to the preceding words by wāw.
verses.115:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse rebukes those who suppose that they will not be resurrected, for this supposition entails that God created them vainly, without an enduring purpose beyond living and dying. The description of God as the True King then provides the argument for resurrection through His transcendence from vanity and falsehood.

God is King, so life, death, sustenance, creation, and resurrection are subject to His binding rule. He is True, so what proceeds from Him is true and contains no vanity. There is no other god to oppose or nullify His rule; and because worship follows lordship, He alone is Lord of the Honorable Throne, the station of authority from which the universe’s governing commands issue. Therefore, all things return to Him and endure through Him: otherwise creation would be vain and the universe false. These four attributes follow the name “Allah,” the Self-existent One who gives existence to all else.

verses.117:
Al-Mizan explains that invoking another god “with Allah” does not mean invoking God and others jointly, since polytheists generally invoked only their supposed partners. It means invoking others despite God’s existence. Duʿāʾ may also mean affirming or believing in another as a god, since such affirmation accompanies invocation.

“He has no proof of this” qualifies “another god”: there is no proof for any other god, but rather proof of the absolute nonexistence of all others. The restriction that his reckoning is only with his Lord is a warning that none can intervene in his divinely determined recompense. It denies intercessors and every other means of deliverance; his punishment in hell will certainly come, and disbelievers will not succeed.
verses.118: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to say the prayer voiced by God’s believing servants in this world, whose faith, request for forgiveness, and appeal for mercy are rewarded with salvation on the Day of Resurrection. The chapter consequently ends as it began, with the success of the believers.
